title: Generative Value Conflicts Reveal LLM Priorities
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A staged automatic pipeline turns a set of values into generated conflict scenarios, model responses, and a ranking of priorities.
layout: 5 stages, left-to-right, arrows between boxes, chat bubbles in evaluation stage
description: A horizontal five-stage flow with a bold title above each stage and black arrows linking them. At far left, a yellow rounded box lists the value set (helpful, harmless, ..., honest). A bracket and arrow lead to two gray boxes, 'Value A: Helpful' and 'Value B: Harmless', joined by a vertical line, which are the sampled pair. An arrow leads to a large gray rounded box holding the LLM-generated conflict scenario. It has a description about optimizing social media for negative reactions, plus Action A and Action B. Next is the open-ended evaluation. A blue user icon has a speech bubble with the prompt, and a blue robot icon replies in a bubble. A bracket then leads to a green box at right with the final value ranking, from 1. harmless to N. helpful.
caption: An example of how the ConflictScope pipeline can be used to evaluate models' value prioritization. Given a set of values of interest, ConflictScope generates realistic value conflicts that an LLM may face in deployment between each pair of values in the value set. By analyzing model behavior across many value conflict scenarios, we can elicit a ranking that reflects the model's prioritization of all values within the value set.
abstract: Past work seeks to align large language model (LLM)-based assistants with a target set of values, but such assistants are frequently forced to make tradeoffs between values when deployed. In response to the scarcity of value conflict in existing alignment datasets, we introduce ConflictScope, an automatic pipeline to evaluate how LLMs prioritize different values. Given a user-defined value set, ConflictScope automatically generates scenarios in which a language model faces a conflict between two values sampled from the set. It then prompts target models with an LLM-written "user prompt" and evaluates their free-text responses to elicit a ranking over values in the value set. Comparing results between multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations, we find that models shift away from supporting protective values, such as harmlessness, and toward supporting personal values, such as user autonomy, in more open-ended value conflict settings. However, including detailed value orderings in models' system prompts improves alignment with a target ranking by 14%, showing that system prompting can achieve moderate success at aligning LLM behavior under value conflict. Our work demonstrates the importance of evaluating value prioritization in models and provides a foundation for future work in this area.
